c01.one_line: Kills the mandate on arithmetic in the first three lines, correctly, and ships two costed reconstructions with it — the anti-optimiser the brief asked for, with a real risk of being a veto machine and near-silence on options.
strengths: Leads with the binding number and it is right: $2,000 ÷ $20/pt = 100 points of lifetime risk against ~430 points of daily ATR, i.e. the account cannot survive one correctly-placed daily stop. This is the finding, and most candidates will bury it under a research plan.

Names the rule-set ambiguity that actually flips the verdict — intraday trailing against peak unrealised equity versus EOD on closed equity — and shows the case (+80 points given back, zero losing trades, account dead) where the same strategy passes under one and fails under the other. Refuses to model without the document.

Knows prop-firm mechanics, not just CME mechanics: consistency rules capping a single day at 30–50% of profit, $3,000 target, scaling plans, the Apex-style trail that locks at initial balance + $100, evaluation-versus-funded divergence, and that most evaluations prohibit overnight and weekend holds — which may end the mandate contractually before it ends arithmetically.

MNQ reconstruction is worked, not gestured at: 1,000 points of room, 0.5-ATR stop ≈ 215 pts = $430 = 21.5% of budget, ~4.6 max-risk losses, $3,000 target = 1,500 net points, ~28 trades at 1.5:1 and 50% win — then concedes the block bootstrap will probably fail this too. Arithmetic checks out and the conclusion is against its own proposal.

Day-one test is the sharpest thing in the submission: measure MAE over the next session from each daily close and read the fraction of nights ≥ 100 points as a first-approximation per-trade probability of account death. That is a falsifiable kill test runnable before any signal research.

Statistical second kill is independent of the first: a daily strategy over 2015–2026 yields 150–400 trades total, so PSR minimum track record length likely exceeds the trade count the strategy will ever produce. Also insists on deflated Sharpe against a disclosed trial count and a declared search budget.

Correctly rejects vectorised daily-bar backtesting under an intraday trailing floor and specifies a tick-ordered event loop, resolving OHLC intrabar ambiguity with ticks — the exact place where a passing backtest becomes a week-one death.

Failure-mode list contains things nobody asked about: back-adjustment artefacts creating signals at roll boundaries, edge concentrated in three FOMC days, stops below 0.3× ATR being fill artefacts rather than edges, and gap risk making the stop notional (one NVDA night = 400–700 NQ points).
concerns: Options are effectively absent. The CEO named IV, skew and the options-to-futures relationship as part of the job; the submission does not mention them once, not even to size into an elevated VXN. Defensible as task-scoped, but it leaves half the brief untested and the candidate's own spec concedes this is the weak side.

Real veto-machine risk. The submission's own predicted outcome is untradeable, its primary reconstruction is predicted to fail too, and the only clearly viable path (intraday MNQ, 40-pt stop = 4% of budget) is one it says is not the strategy asked for. The self-awareness about this is genuine but self-awareness is not a shipped strategy.

No edge hypothesis anywhere. Entirely process and constraint; nothing about what on NQ might actually pay — trend persistence, overnight drift, vol-regime conditioning. The brief did ask for approach rather than an idea, so this is a gap in evidence rather than a demonstrated deficiency, but it is the one thing the assessment cannot see.

Several load-bearing figures are asserted rather than derived: 410–450 ATR, NQ margin $25–30k, earnings-week ATR expansion of 20–35%, ~$4/RT. Each is flagged as needing re-measurement and none is used without that caveat, which is the correct handling, but the whole verdict rests on the ATR number holding.

Much of the structure restates the candidate's own standing framework; the genuinely new work is the MNQ trade-path arithmetic, the MAE kill test and the sample-size argument. A shorter memo with those three items would be more decision-useful than the full nine-phase walk.
Closing offer to publish a shareable page is off-register for a CEO reading a written approach.
c01.distinctive: It converts the account rule document into an arithmetic constraint before touching price data, and then argues against its own preferred rescue — the MNQ reconstruction is costed to the point where it admits that probably fails too. Most candidates will treat $2,000 on a $50k account as a risk-management detail and go hunting for a daily signal; this one treats it as the answer, and independently produces a second kill on statistical grounds (trade count versus minimum track record length) that does not depend on the first being right.
c01.best_used_for: Front-of-project feasibility screens on prop-account and size-constrained mandates, and adversarial validation of strategies someone else built — tick-ordered simulation of trailing-drawdown rule sets, purged walk-forward, block bootstrap over losing streaks, and trial-count-adjusted significance. The right person to hand a backtest that looks good and ask what is wrong with it.
c01.interview_probe: Assume I give you the rule document and it says static end-of-day $2,000 drawdown, overnight holds permitted — the friendliest version of the account. Now bring me a strategy you would actually put on: name the specific edge hypothesis on NQ or MNQ, say why it should exist economically, and tell me how you get past the sample-size problem you just raised — because if 150–400 trades can never clear minimum track record length, that argument kills every daily strategy you will ever test, including the ones that work.

c02.one_line: Leads with a correct, arithmetically-grounded refusal of the mandate as written, backs it with real NQ mechanics and honest statistics, and is the rare candidate whose failure mode is over-caution rather than over-fitting.
strengths: Opens with the binding constraint rather than a strategy idea: $2,000 ÷ $20/pt = 100 points of total room, ~0.25 ATR. Arithmetic is correct, the ATR figure is explicitly flagged as remembered-and-to-be-verified rather than quoted as fact, and the verdict is delivered without a rescue attempt.

Contract mechanics are specific and correct where checkable — $20/pt NQ, 0.25 tick, $5/tick, MNQ $2/pt, Sunday 18:00 ET open, 17:00–18:00 daily break, quarterly Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec with roll at volume crossover ~8 days before third-Friday expiry.

The NQ-vs-MNQ cost comparison (~0.7 vs ~1.1 points round-turn friction, decomposed into commission and one tick per side) is the right calculation expressed in the right unit, and pre-empts the standard objection to micros. Very few candidates will do this unprompted.

Reframes the objective correctly: not Sharpe but P(reach target before absorbing floor). Follows through with Monte Carlo over trade orderings and pass-rate scored separately under EOD and intraday trailing — and refuses to guess which rule applies.
Power analysis is done, not name-dropped: t ≈ SR·√T means true Sharpe 0.5 needs ~16 years, i.e. the entire NQ history. Accepting "underpowered" as a finding is the correct and unusual conclusion.
Separates roll methods by purpose — difference-adjusted for signals, per-contract unadjusted for P&L — and commits to verifying across two rolls for phantom gaps.
Catches that intraday trailing drawdown cannot be scored off daily bars because peak-unrealised trailing is path-dependent. This kills most naive daily-bar prop backtests and almost nobody raises it.

Names its own failure signals and invites the CEO to police them (single-parameter results, equity curve in place of a statistic, Sharpe without variant count), plus states default worst-case assumptions it will proceed under if it gets no answers.
concerns: The CEO's spec list explicitly named margin, and margin appears nowhere in the submission. On a $50k prop account it is not binding, but omitting it entirely from a mechanics-first answer is a gap against the stated checklist.

The options side is a list of correct nouns — VXN term structure, 25-delta risk reversal, gamma-by-strike, variance risk premium — with no actual reasoning demonstrated about how the NQ surface behaves. Depth is asserted, not shown. Defensible given the candidate scoped options down deliberately, but unverified.

Minor internal inconsistency in the power argument: its own math shows true Sharpe 0.5 reaches t=2 over the available history, then it claims sub-0.8 cannot be validated. Probably meant post-deflation, but it didn't say so, and this is exactly the kind of slip it would flag in someone else.

The core verdict is declared in paragraph two, before the Phase 2 adverse-excursion work that is supposed to establish it. The confidence is almost certainly warranted and it is caveated, but the structure is conclusion-then-evidence in a way that could become a habit of pre-judging.

Fluency across the full complex is thinner than the CEO asked for — ES/MES appear only as a relative-vol hypothesis, with no engagement with why one might use ES mechanics as a comparison or a hedge leg.
Timeline friction: a "defensible decision within three weeks" sits awkwardly against a 40-trade paper-forward gate on a daily-timeframe strategy, which is months of calendar time. Unreconciled.

Real risk of producing excellent analysis and never a tradeable strategy. Every incentive in this submission points toward the honest negative result, which is what was asked for, but the CEO should confirm it can also carry something through to a positive, sized, deployable conclusion.
The closing offer to publish it as a shareable page is off-register for a technical submission and reads as pitch rather than analysis.
c02.distinctive: It converts the mandate into a first-passage-probability problem against a path-dependent absorbing barrier and then refuses it on arithmetic in the first paragraph — before touching a signal, and without a parameter search. Most candidates will accept the $2,000/NQ framing and hand back a backtest; this one identifies that the account, not the market, is what makes the mandate fail, and names the four specific exits with a ranked recommendation and the cost objection already pre-empted.
c02.best_used_for: Killing bad mandates early and auditing other people's backtests. It is the right agent to hand a strategy someone else believes in and ask what is wrong with it — cost model, roll adjustment, variant count, path-dependent drawdown scoring, sample power — and to own the risk-sizing and survival-modelling layer under any strategy the firm actually trades.
c02.interview_probe: Assume I answer every question: EOD trail, locks at +$2,000, MNQ approved, full data budget. Now bring me the strongest daily-timeframe edge you actually believe in, sized and costed, and tell me what expectancy and pass rate you expect — I want to see whether you can carry something to a positive conclusion, or whether 'underpowered' is where every project you run ends up.

c03.one_line: Reframes the mandate as a barrier-crossing problem and shows with correct NQ arithmetic that $2,000 of room is a quarter of one ATR — the strongest feasibility-first read you are likely to get, with a real day-one deliverable attached.
strengths: Feasibility arithmetic is done first and is correct: $2,000 ÷ $20/pt = 100 points ≈ 0.24 of a 400–450pt 14-day ATR, with the ATR explicitly flagged as a stale reference needing re-pull. Overnight Globex range alone exceeds the account's lifetime room.

Reframes the objective correctly: the eval is not a Sharpe problem but P(+$3,000 before −$2,000), and gives the honest zero-edge baseline of 2000/5000 = 40%. Most candidates will optimise the wrong objective.

The MNQ argument is the non-obvious correct one. He kills the usual 'micros give more room' claim — dollar barriers are unchanged, so the ratio and the 40% are unchanged — and identifies granularity (5–8 bets instead of 1) as the only real benefit, and only for a real edge.

Product-specific traps that demonstrate hands-on work, not reading: CME equity-index settlement is the VWAP of the last 30 seconds of RTH and is therefore not a tradeable fill; the trade day is 17:00→16:00 ET so a UTC-midnight bar cut manufactures gaps a breakout system will trade; additive back-adjustment can drive a 25-year NQ series negative and silently break every percentage-return and z-score feature.

Correct cost arithmetic ($5.00/tick NQ, $0.50 MNQ, ~2.7 ticks ≈ 0.68 points RT) followed by the unusual honesty of saying cost is NOT the binding constraint here, then relocating the real cost to stop-order slippage through an overnight gap. He declines an easy kill that would have looked rigorous.

Distinguishes the eval trail (EOD, closed balance) from the funded trail (intraday, peak unrealised) and insists both rule sets be simulated on every candidate, because a strategy can pass one and die on the other. Names Topstep vs Apex terms as the specific ambiguity and refuses to guess.

Options used in the concrete direction the CEO asked for: Black-76 on DataMine settlement IVs, implied 1-day move placed beside the 100-point stop to get the stop-out probability before any backtest, and 25-delta risk reversal used to argue ATR-symmetric sizing understates the downside gap tail.

Gives a decision, not just a test — MNQ with daily signals and flat overnight, 15–20% odds an edge survives the battery, 45–55% pass probability against a 40% baseline — and says plainly that this is a thin improvement over a coin flip.

Day-one deliverable is concrete and checkable (MAE histogram of random-entry 1- and 3-day adverse excursion vs the 100-point floor), with a 5-day go/no-go gate and explicit pass thresholds written in advance.
concerns: 'The deployment sample size is one trade' is rhetorically strong but not literally right, and he half-knows it: he notes the trail locks at +$2,000, which means early profits create real buffer and more than one draw. The overstatement is in service of the conclusion he already reached.

The 40% zero-edge baseline ignores costs, the ~$1,000 daily loss limit, minimum trading days and consistency rules — all of which drag it below 40%. He lists those rules as unknowns but never adjusts the number he leads with.

Margin is never mentioned, despite the CEO naming it explicitly among the specs he wants known cold. Roll mechanics are handled as a data-artefact problem but the actual roll convention and volume migration timing are never stated.

Several load-bearing numbers are priors, not results: 'I expect 85–95%' on the MAE histogram, '>90%' floor-breach for any daily-hold configuration. Labelled as priors, but the verdict is effectively pre-announced and the research plan is shaped to confirm it.

A meaningful fraction of the submission is the candidate's own operating checklist restated (pre-registration, DSR/PBO/CSCV/Newey–West, three roll series). The genuinely new content is concentrated in the arithmetic, the barrier framing and the NQ-specific traps; the middle phases are boilerplate.
Self-declared weakness is real: the natural output is a graveyard. Mitigations are stated but unproven — nothing here demonstrates he can generate a hypothesis worth killing, only that he kills well.
c03.distinctive: He does not answer the question as asked. He establishes that the mandate is arithmetically unsound before touching signal work, then rebuilds the question as a barrier-crossing problem with a stated zero-edge baseline — and separately, he declines an available kill on cost when the arithmetic does not support it, which is the tell that he is reasoning rather than reciting scepticism.
c03.best_used_for: Last gate before capital: feasibility arithmetic on account and drawdown rule sets, forensic teardown of strategies that look good on paper (roll artefacts, settlement-as-fill, intrabar optimism, multiple testing), and building the honest event-driven fill and path-risk simulation that vectorised frameworks get wrong.
c03.interview_probe: You have told me this mandate is probably infeasible and given me a 15–20% estimate that any edge survives your battery. Now give me the NQ daily hypothesis you would actually test first — the specific signal, why you believe it has a structural reason to exist on this index rather than ES, and what you would expect its expectancy in ticks to be before you run it. If your answer is that you would not propose one until the data is in, tell me what I am paying you to generate rather than reject.

c04.one_line: Opens by killing the mandate on arithmetic — $2,000 / $20 per point = 100 NQ points against a 250–450 point daily ATR — then lays out a day-one plan that would deliver a defensible verdict inside a week; strongest futures-mechanics candidate so far, weakest on options.
strengths: Leads with the binding constraint rather than a strategy idea: the whole drawdown budget is ~0.25–0.4x one day's ordinary range, so the implied per-trade stop is noise on a daily bar. This is exactly the 'tell me it doesn't work and why' behaviour the brief asked for, and it arrives in the first paragraph.

Contract and eval mechanics are correct and load-bearing, not decorative: $20/point, 0.25 tick = $5.00, H/M/U/Z, cash settlement to the third-Friday SOQ, liquidity migrating around the Thursday eight days prior, settlement off the 15:59:30–16:00:00 window. It also knows the real prop terms — ~$3,000 target against $2,000 trailing — and turns that into a first-passage problem with absorbing barriers that is computable before any price data is touched.

Identifies the underspecified term that actually decides the outcome — EOD-close trail vs intraday-unrealized trail, ratcheting or locking — shows the consequence concretely (a +150 trade giving back 80 spends 80% of the budget while winning), and refuses to choose, escalating it instead.

Names failure modes the brief did not ask about: back-adjusted continuous series manufacturing level-based breakout signals, gap-through stop fills rather than fills at the stop price, and Nasdaq-100 top-heavy constituent concentration making a daily NQ hold a scheduled megacap-earnings position rather than a tail risk.

Raises statistical power as a first-class problem — 100–200 trades over eight years cannot separate a true Sharpe of 0.8 from zero — and pairs it with pre-registration, a variant counter, deflated Sharpe, PBO via CSCV, purged/embargoed walk-forward and a locked 18-month holdout. It also lists what would make it distrust its own good-looking result.

Explicitly marks what is measured versus remembered: flags not knowing today's ATR as a day-one measurement, labels the overnight-move prior as HYPOTHESIS (UNTESTED), and says it will re-verify margin and fees against the current spec sheet with a date rather than cite from memory.
concerns: It announces the verdict — NOT TRADEABLE — before running the Phase 1 Monte Carlo that is supposed to establish it. The arithmetic is sound and the conclusion is very probably right, but committing to the answer in advance is the mirror image of the overfitting failure the CEO fears: a candidate who has decided may not look hard for the configuration that survives.

The $25–35k 'minimum viable account size' is asserted without derivation. It is plausible, but it arrives with the same authority as the 100-point calculation that was shown in full, and the candidate's own standard is to never present a number it did not compute.

'Can fail 60% of paths under intraday-unrealized trailing' is an uncomputed illustrative figure. Hedged with 'can', but it is precisely the kind of confident number the rest of the submission disciplines itself against.

Options are almost absent. One line about a defined-risk NQ structure — a genuinely good observation, and honest about prop firms forbidding it — but no demonstration of IV, skew or vol-spread reasoning. The task was futures-only so the penalty is limited, but the CEO's secondary requirement is untested by this sample.

Substantial stretches restate the candidate's own operating checklist rather than reason about this mandate. The nine-phase plan and the 'Me' self-critique paragraph in particular read as process recitation; the genuinely new thinking is concentrated in the opening arithmetic and the failure-mode section.

Long for what was asked. The CEO said 'talk me through how you would approach it' and got a document. It is well-structured and scannable, but a version half this length would be more decision-useful, and the closing offer to publish a shareable page is noise in an interview answer.
c04.distinctive: It treats the mandate itself as the deliverable to test, and does the killing arithmetic before touching data — then still specifies the full research pipeline it would run if it turns out to be wrong, and names the four concrete escape routes (MNQ, shorter horizon, bigger budget, or a stated-low-probability lottery ticket) rather than just refusing. Most candidates will either propose a strategy or wave at 'risk management'; this one shows the number that makes the brief impossible and separates 'passing the evaluation' from 'having an edge' as distinct products the CEO might be buying.
c04.best_used_for: Front-loaded feasibility work and adversarial review of futures strategies: sizing a mandate against contract mechanics and drawdown geometry before research spend, auditing someone else's backtest for roll-adjustment artefacts, fill-model optimism and multiple-testing inflation, and writing the honest negative result. Would need a second analyst or a structured prompt to carry the options-pricing side of the role.
c04.interview_probe: You put the minimum viable account size at $25–35k for a one-lot daily NQ position. Derive it on the spot — what structural stop, at what ATR, over what losing streak, and what happens to that number if ATR doubles? Then: if your Phase 1 Monte Carlo came back saying the mandate is achievable at a modest per-trade edge, would you actually pursue it, or have you already decided?

c05.one_line: Exactly the analyst the brief asks for — kills the mandate on arithmetic in the first paragraph with the right numbers — but is built to kill strategies far more readily than to ship one.
strengths: Leads with the binding constraint and gets the arithmetic right: $2,000 / ($20 × 1) = 100 points against a 410–450 point ATR, i.e. the entire account buffer is ~0.23 of one day's range, and correctly notes that a trailing rule moves the wall up rather than building a cushion. This is the answer, and it arrives before any signal talk.

Reframes the problem correctly: an evaluation is 10–25 daily trades, so pass/fail is dominated by sequence variance — 'a first-passage survival problem under a path-dependent barrier, not a strategy-selection problem.' Most candidates will treat this as a strategy search.

Real prop-firm specificity rather than generic 'drawdown rules': distinguishes Topstep-style EOD trail locking at start+$100 from Apex-style intraday trail, and gives the concrete consequence (open trade +80 then back to flat permanently spends 80 of 100 points while earning nothing). Also flags that many evaluations bar overnight holds at all, which would terminate a daily mandate by rule, not by arithmetic.

Contract mechanics are carried, not looked up: $20/point NQ, 0.25 tick, Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec, volume/OI crossover roll ~3–5 sessions before third Friday, 17:00 ET boundary, VXN rather than VIX because NQ is the product, earnings-week ATR expansion of 20–35%.

Catches a trap most will miss: NQ was in the low thousands a decade ago, so any point-denominated threshold is comparing incommensurable things across its own history — everything in ATR or percent units. Also carries dual series (back-adjusted for signals, unadjusted per-contract for PnL and stop placement) and refuses to compute stop-hits from daily bars.

Validation discipline is genuinely top-decile: pre-registered regime taxonomy with breakpoints from a burn-in window rather than full-sample quantiles, deflated Sharpe with a stated trial count, PBO via CSCV, stationary block bootstrap, and an explicit evidence bar (fewer than five independent episodes across two calendar years = INCONCLUSIVE, positive or negative).

States a falsifier for its own headline claim with a measurement and a deadline: under ~2% of sessions gapping beyond 100 points plus positive conditional expectancy in four of the pre-registered vol cells, by end of day one. It commits to being checkable.

Names its own worst failure mode — 'a new regime' explaining every live drawdown — and attaches a mechanical remedy (regime-attribution debt: state the forward-observable condition and the date by which performance should resume, or the story was wrong in writing and the strategy retires). Rare and load-bearing.
Refuses to quietly substitute MNQ for the NQ the CEO specified; puts it up as the CEO's business decision instead.
concerns: Arithmetic slip in the MNQ line: written as `1000 / (2 × 1) = 1,000 points`. The answer is right for a $2,000 budget but the equation as printed is wrong twice over, and it sits three paragraphs below a candidate who has just staked its credibility on doing arithmetic first. Minor in substance, but by the candidate's own published standard it is exactly the kind of thing that should not reach the CEO.

Possible domain error dressed as a headline risk. NQ trades ~23 hours; true gaps are confined to the Friday-close-to-Sunday-open window and the thin 17:00–18:00 ET break. The dominant overnight risk is continuous session movement, where a resting stop does fill, albeit with slippage. The submission says 'the stop is not a stop across the break' and makes the gap distribution its primary kill test — the conclusion may still hold via overnight range, but the mechanism named is arguably the wrong one.

Structurally biased toward the negative. Eight phases, seven blocking questions to the CEO, and an entire refusal list before any strategy exists. The CEO wants strategies developed and tested as well as killed; nothing here demonstrates what this analyst does on day forty when the arithmetic clears and an actual edge has to be found. Self-admits being 'slow relative to what a trading desk needs.'

Much of the submission is a faithful projection of the candidate's own charter — Phases 2 through 8 restate its operating principles nearly clause for clause. The task-specific thinking (gap test, first-passage framing, ATR-unit thresholds, sequence variance) is genuinely good but occupies maybe a third of the page; the rest is recital. Worth testing whether the frame adapts to a problem it was not pre-written for.

Options coverage is thin in practice — one phase asking whether the PnL is short vol in disguise. Defensible given a futures-only task, but the CEO named options reasoning as a requirement and this submission gives almost no evidence of it beyond naming 25-delta risk reversal once.
Everything is promised, nothing is demonstrated. No number here has been computed from data; the ATR figure is self-flagged as needing re-measurement. The plan is excellent; execution is unevidenced.
Closes with an unprompted offer to publish a shareable page — small, but it is sales gloss on a document that otherwise earns attention by being unornamented.
c05.distinctive: It converts the mandate into a survival-probability problem under a path-dependent barrier and answers it from arithmetic in the first paragraph, then keeps going and names the one thing that would prove it wrong, with a date. Most candidates will spend the page describing a backtesting pipeline; this one has already decided the mandate is probably dead, said so plainly, priced the four alternatives, and left the product decision with the CEO rather than quietly swapping to MNQ.
c05.best_used_for: Front-of-funnel triage and adversarial review: killing unsound mandates within hours, pre-registering regime taxonomies and success criteria before anyone touches data, and tearing down a strategy someone else is enthusiastic about — deflated Sharpe with the real trial count, episode counts per cell, breach probability under both trail rules. Also the right person to own the prop-account survival modelling specifically. Not the person to hand a blank page and 'find me an edge by Friday.'
c05.interview_probe: Your kill test is the close-to-open gap distribution — but NQ trades nearly 23 hours a day, so the only real gaps are Friday-to-Sunday and the 17:00–18:00 maintenance break. Walk me through what actually happens to a resting stop at 09:00 CET during a Globex selloff, and tell me whether your 100-point kill argument survives once you replace 'gap' with 'overnight session range plus slippage.' Then: suppose the arithmetic clears on MNQ and I give you six weeks — what is the first strategy hypothesis you test, and why that one?

c06.one_line: Exceptional ruin-and-validation discipline with genuine contract-spec fluency; the risk is an analyst who kills mandates rigorously but never ships a strategy.
strengths: Leads with the arithmetic the CEO cares about and gets it right: $2,000 / $20 per point = 100 points of total account life, framed as cumulative adverse excursion from the high-water mark rather than per-trade risk, then compared against session ATR. This is the single most decision-useful paragraph any candidate could write for this mandate.

Contract specs are cold and correct — NQ $20/pt and $5/tick, MNQ $2/pt, 0.25 grid, the 18:00–17:00 ET Globex daily bar versus the 09:30–16:00 RTH bar, the 17:00–18:00 maintenance break. It also correctly reconstructs Topstep-style $50k combine mechanics from memory: floor starts at $48,000, trails the equity high, locks at $50,000 once equity reaches $52,000, with a $1,000 daily loss limit and $3,000 target as stated assumptions.

The back-adjustment analysis is the strongest piece of original domain reasoning in the submission: ~24,000 index at ~4.5% rates minus ~0.7% yield gives roughly 200+ points of quarterly carry, so a back-adjusted continuous series drifts on the order of 800 points/year against tradable prices — set against a 100-point budget, that is phantom PnL, not a rounding error. Its fix (ratio-adjusted for signal research, unadjusted per-contract for fill and PnL simulation) is the right one.

Identifies the project's actual killer failure mode unprompted: an intraday tick-by-tick trailing drawdown cannot be evaluated on daily bars, because a trade that closes +40 after being −180 at 11:15 is a winner on daily bars and a blown account in reality. It commits to 1-minute path data and to reporting EOD-trail and intraday-trail as two separate strategies with two separate ruin probabilities.

Points-versus-ATR non-stationarity is a subtle trap most candidates will miss — NQ ATR was 60–120 points in 2015 and 400+ now, so a fixed 100-point budget has lost roughly 5× of its room and any points-based backtest across that span will look far safer than it is. Its fix (express thresholds in ATR units, convert at the simulated regime's vol drawn from a fitted EGARCH) is coherent.

Overfitting controls are named, specific and correctly matched to the problem: declared trial budget written down before testing, deflated Sharpe against that count, PBO via CSCV, Hansen SPA against the whole trial family rather than the winner, purged walk-forward with embargo. It explicitly counts instrument and timeframe selection as trials that inflate the count — a discipline most people skip.

Surfaces two risks nobody asked about. First, that the objective may be wrong: if the evaluation costs a fee and can be reset, the right objective is P(pass) net of fees over a sequence of attempts, which may favour higher variance and has a different optimum from Sharpe — and it flags this as the CEO's call rather than silently optimising. Second, that rule interactions (consistency caps, minimum trading days, flat-by-time) can fail an account that never touches the floor, and that a low-frequency daily strategy is especially exposed to the minimum-trading-days constraint.

Writes falsification thresholds before live trading rather than after: live per-trade MAE inside the simulated distribution via KS test at 20 trades, realised slippage measured against assumption, realised ATR inside the validated band with the strategy declared out of scope rather than 'under pressure' if it exits. It also hands the CEO a list of failure signals to police it by.

Declares its own microstructure blindness and defers correctly: if someone with floor experience disputes a fill assumption, its prior is that they are right and it fetches tick data rather than arguing from the model.
concerns: It reaches a hard conclusion — 'there is no contract-and-size combination under a $2,000 trailing drawdown that supports a genuine daily-horizon structural stop' — before pulling a single row of data, resting on an N ≥ 8–10 stops-to-ruin requirement that is asserted rather than derived and on ATR figures quoted from memory. Directionally the arithmetic is sound, but a candidate whose whole thesis is 'do not be confidently wrong' should not state its central negative verdict this firmly one section before it says it would go measure the inputs.

Several headline numbers are unsourced recall presented in the register of fact: NQ 14-day ATR '410–450', NQ/ES range ratio '1.3–1.5×', earnings-week range inflation '+20–35%', 'exceeded on roughly a third of days'. These are the load-bearing inputs to the feasibility verdict and none carries a date, a source or an interval, which is exactly the standard the candidate imposes on everyone else.

The options side is visibly book-learned and contains a real error. It proposes 'OPRA or CBOE DataShop for the NQ chain' — options on NQ futures are a CME product and do not disseminate through OPRA; that data comes from CME DataMine or Databento GLBX. It also treats VXN as having a term structure comparable to VIX, when VXN has no listed futures curve. Black-76 on the future rather than Black-Scholes on the index is correctly stated, and the observation that a defined-risk vertical caps terminal loss but the long leg's intraday mark still moves the trail is genuinely sharp — but the plumbing underneath is not verified.

The roll description is sloppy where the rest is exact: 'the Thursday before the second Friday of Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec' is not the CME equity index roll, which runs eight days before the third-Friday expiry. It hedges by saying it would verify against volume, which saves it operationally, but the folklore it quoted is itself wrong.

Loose money language in one place that matters: 1 MNQ at a 1-ATR stop risking $850 is described as '42.5% of the entire account'. It is 42.5% of the $2,000 drawdown budget and 1.7% of the $50,000 account. The point survives — the budget is what is absorbing — but a trading analyst conflating account size with drawdown budget in a sentence about sizing is the kind of slip that propagates.

Everything downstream is gated on a rule PDF the candidate does not have, and the entire first-day plan is contingent on reading it. That is correct practice, but the CEO should expect the first deliverable to be a question list plus a feasibility memo, not analysis of a strategy.

The submission is a very close structural reading of the candidate's own operating charter — the phase order, the reporting contract, the refusals, the stated failure modes and several of the numbers all pre-exist the task. It adapts them well and adds genuine new work (the carry arithmetic, the N-to-ruin table, the Topstep reconstruction, the parallel-evaluations reframe), but the CEO is seeing a method applied more than a mind improvising, and should test whether the method bends when the problem does not fit it.

Nothing in the submission demonstrates the candidate can generate or evaluate a strategy hypothesis — the task did not ask for one, so this is not a deduction, but the entire toolkit on display is survival analysis and validation. There is no evidence of edge discovery, feature construction, or a view on what actually drives NQ.
c06.distinctive: It converts the mandate into a first-passage problem with an absorbing boundary and solves for probability of ruin and probability of reaching the lock, rather than producing a backtest — and it brings a catastrophe-reinsurance tail toolkit (POT/GPD with mean-residual-life threshold selection, Bühlmann–Straub credibility weighting of a thin loss sample against a prior built from the instrument's own range distribution, expected shortfall at 97.5%, Kaplan–Meier survival with confidence bands) that almost no trading-analyst candidate will have. The specific insight that a trailing drawdown tightens with every dollar earned until the lock, and that the pre-lock gauntlet is the dominant term in pass probability, is the correct framing of this problem and is rarely stated this plainly.
c06.best_used_for: Pre-mortem feasibility rulings and independent validation: deciding in an afternoon whether a proposed mandate, account size or drawdown budget is arithmetically survivable, and auditing strategies other people built — trial-count deflation, PBO, walk-forward integrity, roll and back-adjustment hygiene, and ruin probability under the actual trailing rule. Treat it as the gate a strategy must pass, not as the source of the strategy.
c06.interview_probe: Assume the rule document comes back and the trail is end-of-day closing balance, not intraday, and the floor locks at $50,000 once equity touches $52,000 — so the arithmetic is less brutal than you assumed. Now give me an actual NQ daily-horizon hypothesis you would test first, say why you believe it has an edge rather than why it might survive, and tell me what in NQ's own behaviour — not in the drawdown maths — would make you abandon it.

c07.one_line: Kills the mandate with correct arithmetic in the first 200 words and backs it with contract-spec detail that can only come from having actually handled this data — but is self-declared not-a-strategist and never demonstrates he can find an edge, only refute one.
strengths: Leads with the binding arithmetic rather than a process: $2,000 / $20 per point = 100 points total, against a ~420-point daily ATR, stated as a ratio (0.24x one day's range) before any data is pulled. This is the single most decision-relevant fact in the mandate and he gets to it first.

Contract mechanics are verifiably correct and specific, not recited: NQ $20/pt and $5.00 tick, MNQ $2/pt and $0.50 tick, quarterly H/M/U/Z, the conventional roll on the Thursday eight days before third-Friday expiry, and the settlement being the ~15:00 CT VWAP window rather than the 16:00 ET print. He also notices unprompted that today is the third Friday of September 2026, that NQU6 settles on this morning's SOQ, and that the roll to NQZ6 went through around Sept 10 — so any continuous file pulled right now spans a live roll.

Sizes the roll gap from first principles — front-end rates above the NDX dividend yield implies roughly 0.7-0.9% of index per quarter, ~150-250 points, $3,000-$5,000 per roll — and then makes the point that lands: one roll gap is larger than the entire drawdown budget, so an unaudited continuous series can produce a backtest whose whole PnL is four phantom jumps a year.

Separates the three things 'daily bar' can mean on NQ (Globex session 18:00-17:00 ET, RTH 09:30-16:00, settle vs close) and commits to building all three and stating which one the result depends on. Most candidates will not notice this is ambiguous at all.

Correctly identifies that the trailing threshold, not trade PnL, is the governing constraint, and that under an intraday trail the binding metric is maximum adverse excursion — a trade that goes +60 and closes +20 still ratchets the floor. Refuses to guess EOD vs intraday and commits to modelling both.

Costs are computed, not waved at: ~$4.30 commission plus one tick per side = $14.30 round turn = 0.72 NQ points, ~$3,575/yr at one trade per session, i.e. 1.8x the entire drawdown budget in friction alone. Concludes any daily rule must clear roughly 3 ticks net before it has done anything.

Statistical honesty is real, not decorative. Trial count declared with every statistic, deflated Sharpe, parameter surface and plateau median rather than the best cell, purged/embargoed walk-forward, block bootstrap, Monte Carlo on trade ordering with P(touch the floor) as a headline metric. The illustrative bootstrap interval he quotes — Sharpe 1.0 on ~250 trades giving roughly [0.2, 1.8] — is arithmetically about right, which suggests he has actually run this rather than named it.

Draws the distinction the CEO asked for in plain words: 'I could not establish an edge' is not 'I proved there isn't one', and he commits to naming the trade count that would settle it and to saying when that count is unreachable so the decision to keep spending is the CEO's.

Puts the prop firm's consistency rule and news restrictions into the simulator as hard constraints rather than commentary, and notes the consistency rule alone forbids the lottery-ticket approach. That is a failure mode that invalidates a passing equity curve and most candidates will not model it.

States a falsifiable prior up front with separated confidence levels — high on the arithmetic, moderate on whether a daily-signal/intraday-executed MNQ variant clears costs — and invites being held to it.
concerns: He is an auditor, not a strategist, and says so. Every phase in the plan is about establishing whether a number means anything; not one line addresses how he would generate a hypothesis worth testing. The CEO's brief asks for someone to develop and test strategies. This candidate is outstanding at the 'test' half and unproven on the 'develop' half, and the whole submission succeeds by refuting a mandate that was probably designed to be refutable — which is the easier win.

The central dichotomy is slightly rigged. He offers only a structural stop (>=150 pts, untradeable) or a budget stop (20-30 pts, a lottery ticket) and says 'there is no parameter setting between those two'. There plainly is: a daily-computed signal executed and exited intraday with a 50-80 point stop sits exactly in the gap he skips, and that is the most obvious way anyone would actually attempt this mandate. He gestures at it later ('daily-signal, intraday-executed') but never brings it back into the table, so the argument reads more airtight than it is.

The ATR figure doing all the work is asserted, not measured. '1.5-1.9% of index, ~380-470 points' is on the high side for a normal NQ regime; at 1.2% the same arithmetic gives ~290 points and the ratio moves from 0.24x to 0.34x. He does flag that he will recompute it, and the conclusion survives either way, but the headline number the CEO will remember is a quoted one.

Timeline is precise where it is cheap and absent where it is expensive. Phase 0 is half a day and Phase 1 is one day; Phases 2 through 8 — the actual research — carry no estimate at all. Given his own documented tendency to build infrastructure instead of answering the question, the unbounded half of the plan is the half that needs the bound.
Options are absent. The task did not ask, so this is not a fault in the submission, but the CEO named options reasoning as part of the role and nothing here evidences it. It remains untested.

Long. The verdict-first structure and tables make it scannable, but there are eight phases, eight failure modes, two tables of asks and four exits — the CEO will get the answer in the first screen and then read three more screens of method. Some of that is the point; some of it is the pipeline-builder showing his hand.
c07.distinctive: Almost anyone can say 'check your roll adjustment'. This candidate sizes the roll gap in dollars against the specific account budget, notices unprompted that today's date sits on a live NQ roll and names the expiring and incoming contract codes, and knows that NQ's daily settle is a 15:00 CT VWAP window rather than the 16:00 ET print. The specificity is checkable and it is right, which is the rarest signal in this pile. He also does the thing the CEO explicitly asked for — arriving at 'this cannot be done as written, here is the arithmetic' inside an hour instead of three weeks — and then lays out four named exits rather than leaving the CEO with a dead end.
c07.best_used_for: Adjudicating whether an existing result is real: auditing a backtest someone else built, rebuilding the data layer under it, localising surprising PnL to specific roll dates or session-boundary artifacts, and reporting survival statistics with the trial count declared. Also the right agent to hand any mandate or account-terms question to before capital or research time is committed — the constraint arithmetic and prop-rule extraction are fast, cheap and exactly what he does well.
c07.interview_probe: Suppose I accept the MNQ recommendation and give you clean, audited data on day one. Give me the first strategy hypothesis you would test, the economic reason you believe it should work on NQ specifically rather than on any liquid index future, and your honest guess at its expectancy in ticks net of costs — no pipeline, no phases, and I do not want a family of rules to sweep. If the answer is a process for choosing a hypothesis rather than a hypothesis, that is the hire's limitation.

c08.one_line: Leads with the arithmetic that kills the mandate ($2,000 = 100 NQ points ≈ a third of one day's ATR), pre-commits to a NO, and offers concrete day-1 deliverables — strongest on futures mechanics and validation discipline, silent on options.
strengths: Opens with range-to-budget arithmetic rather than a strategy idea: $20/point, $5/tick, 100 points of total drawdown against a 220–330 point ATR, and states the implied stop sits inside the overnight gap distribution. This is the exact failure the CEO asked to be told about, delivered before any data is touched.

Identifies the load-bearing unknown the brief omitted — intraday unrealized-peak trail vs EOD closed-balance trail — and shows why it flips the answer (a +80 trade closing +20 burns $1,200 with no losing trade). Also surfaces daily loss limit, contract cap, minimum trading days and the consistency rule, none of which were in the mandate.

Phase 1 zero-edge survival simulation: derive P(breach) for random entries under the encoded trail, then invert to a required (win rate, payoff, frequency) surface that any hypothesis must clear. This kills most ideas without a backtest and is a genuinely unusual sequencing choice.

Correctly separates feature construction on back-adjusted series from execution on unadjusted per-contract prices, on the grounds that back-adjusted prices produce fictional point-based stop levels. Most candidates will not mention roll stitching at all.

Validation is pre-registered and falsifiable: append-only trial ledger, capped trial budget, purged k-fold with embargo ≥ label horizon, CPCV, PBO, deflated Sharpe, single-use holdout, and an explicit underpowered threshold (<100 trades) with the honest observation that daily NQ yields ~400 trades over 10 years across ~4 regimes.

States its own failure mode as a checkable number ('the number to check when you doubt me is the trial count') and lists the specific tells the CEO should stop it on — pass threshold renegotiated after results, holdout mentioned twice, 'a slightly wider stop'.
Answers unanswered questions with stated defaults (harshest plausible trail reading, $4 round-turn, one tick slippage, two ticks on stop exits) so work is not blocked on the CEO.
concerns: Zero options content. The CEO explicitly asked for reasoning about implied vol, skew and how ES/NQ options relate to the futures; the submission never mentions IV, VXN, skew or the variance risk premium even as context features. The task was futures-only, so this is a fair omission, but it leaves half the brief untested.

The MNQ counter-proposal is only half-costed. It computes the drawdown side (1,000 points ≈ 4 ATR of room) but never checks the other side of the eval: whether 1 MNQ at $2/point can reach the profit target within the minimum trading days. An eval that cannot be passed for lack of upside fails just as hard as one that breaches; the profit target appears only on the list of things to request.

'Front-month volume migrates the Thursday before the third Friday' is loose — the CME equity index roll conventionally happens roughly eight days before expiry, i.e. the Thursday before the second Friday. Small, but it is the kind of specific the CEO said he would check.

The López de Prado stack (triple-barrier, sample uniqueness, CPCV, PBO, deflated Sharpe) is recited nearly verbatim and is heavy machinery for ~40 daily trades a year. The candidate concedes the power problem but does not adapt the toolkit to it; there is a risk of ceremony substituting for a result.

Process-forward. The plan has seven phases, a rulebook dependency and a data-budget dependency before a single hypothesis is tested. The day-1 list is concrete enough to mitigate this, but an engagement that ends in a well-documented NO after three weeks is only valuable if the counter-proposal arrives with it — and that counter-proposal is currently a sketch.
Predicts its own verdict before seeing data. This is defensible here because the arithmetic carries it, but it is also a commitment that could make a contrary finding harder to report.
Closing offer to publish a shareable page reads as pitch rather than analysis.
c08.distinctive: It treats the prop drawdown rule as the binding constraint and turns it into a feasibility test that runs before any signal research — encode the trail as a function, simulate a zero-edge strategy against it, and derive the required-edge surface. Most candidates will answer this brief with a backtesting methodology; this one answers it with arithmetic that makes the backtest unnecessary, and separately gets the unadjusted-prices-for-stops detail right.
c08.best_used_for: Killing mandates and strategies that do not survive their own constraints: feasibility arithmetic on account terms, encoding prop firm rules into path-dependent survival simulations, and auditing whether an existing backtest's Sharpe survives trial count, roll method, costs and a tick-by-tick trailing floor. Good as the person who tells you which strategies are not worth building; less proven as the person who originates the one that is.
c08.interview_probe: You've told me the NQ-daily mandate fails and that MNQ is the way out — now finish that arithmetic: at $2/point with a $3,000 profit target, minimum trading days and a consistency rule, what expectancy and trade frequency does one MNQ need to pass the eval before it breaches, and does any of the mechanisms you listed plausibly deliver it? If the answer is no, say so and tell me what's left.

c09.one_line: Near-exact fit: reframes the mandate as a first-passage problem, shows the 100-points-of-room arithmetic that likely kills it, and knows NQ specs and prop-eval rule structures cold — options coverage is the one thin spot.
strengths: Leads with the binding arithmetic rather than a strategy idea: $2,000 ÷ ($20 × 1) = 100 points against a ~400-450 point NQ ATR, i.e. the whole drawdown budget is a quarter of one ordinary day. That is the correct first move and most candidates will open with an idea instead.

Correctly identifies that the objective function in the brief is wrong. A prop evaluation with a moving floor is a first-passage problem — maximise P(target before floor) — not a Sharpe problem, and those have different optima. Proposes being measured on ΔP(pass) over a zero-edge baseline.

The intraday-trail insight is both non-obvious and arithmetically right: under a trail on unrealized equity highs, a trade that runs +150 and closes +40 has moved the floor past the close and killed the account. Correctly concludes that wide-stop daily trend-following is mechanically self-destructive under that rule and fine under an EOD trail, and refuses to guess which applies.

Contract mechanics are accurate and current, not recited generically: $20/point, $5.00/tick, Globex 18:00–17:00 ET with the 17:00–18:00 halt, RTH 09:30–16:00, settlement from the 14:59:30–15:00:00 CT window, H/M/U/Z cash-settled to the SOQ, and the correct live front month (NQZ6, with NQU6 expiring today). Also correct that NQ's inside book is thin relative to ES but that one lot clears it.

Knows prop-eval rule structure beyond the four numbers given: infers the likely ~$1,000 daily loss limit, contract cap, minimum trading days, reset fee, and — the genuinely sharp one — the consistency rule, noting that a positive-skew daily strategy making its money in three sessions of sixty passes the drawdown rule and fails the payout rule.

Roll handling is specific and correctly reasoned: volume-crossover roll, two series (ratio-adjusted for signals, unadjusted per-contract for PnL), with the right explanation of why back-adjustment over a long NQ history corrupts percentage-based calculations. Commits to plotting seams and reconciling a sample month by hand.

The zero-edge coin-flipper simulation under the account's actual rules is the best single idea in the submission: one day of work that gives every later result a denominator and prices what the reset fee is actually buying.

Anti-overfitting discipline is concrete, not slogan-level: trial count logged beside every Sharpe, deflated Sharpe and PBO via CSCV, split committed to a file before running, hold-out run once, sharp parameter peak treated as noise and plateau as signal, costs attached from the first run so no frictionless number anchors judgement.
Labels every recalled figure as recalled and pending measurement, and states defaults for each open question so work does not stall waiting on the CEO.
concerns: The [arithmetic] tag is applied to claims that are not arithmetic. 'Daily timeframe and prop evaluation may be structurally incompatible' and 'the binding constraint is probably not the one you named' are inferences about a rule document not yet read. The tagging system exists to separate measurement from opinion; using the harder tag on the softer claim borrows authority it has not earned, and it is the one place the submission does what the CEO warned against.

Pre-announces the likely verdict — 'DEAD on arithmetic' — before measuring the ATR it rests on. Defensible as an expected-value statement, but it anchors the research it is about to commission, which is the exact mechanism the candidate criticises elsewhere (never run a frictionless pass first because the number anchors judgement).

Options are essentially absent. One sentence gestures that passing an evaluation 'is an options-pricing problem' and does not develop it, and nothing addresses IV, skew, or the ES/NQ vol surface. The task was futures-only so this is partly the prompt's doing, but the CEO named options as part of the job and there was room to show a read on it.

Time-to-first-strategy is long. Day 1 is a memo, week 1 is a baseline, weeks 3–4 are characterisation, and a verdict on an actual hypothesis lands at weeks 6–8. The characterisation pack has standalone value and the candidate says so, but a desk that needs a tradeable candidate sooner should set that expectation now.

The stated known weakness — demanding a burden of proof no research programme can meet, producing a desk that trades nothing — is real, self-diagnosed, and only partly mitigated. The veto-rate tracking is a good instrument but it is self-reported and lagging.

Volume of output. It is well organised and scannable, but the CEO asked how the candidate would work the problem and got roughly nine sections. A shorter version with the same content would be stronger, and the closing offer to publish a shareable page is padding.
c09.distinctive: Reframes the objective function rather than answering the question as asked: recognises that a trailing floor makes this an absorbing-barrier / first-passage problem, derives the consequence that maximum favourable excursion becomes a liability under an unrealized-equity trail, and proposes a zero-edge coin-flipper baseline so that every subsequent result has a denominator. Most candidates will describe a competent backtesting pipeline; this one questions whether the mandate is arithmetically survivable and prices the answer.
c09.best_used_for: Front-loaded feasibility work and killing bad mandates cheaply: turning account rules into hard constraints, characterising NQ/ES behaviour into reusable reference artifacts, and auditing other people's backtests for roll artifacts, trial-count inflation, fill fantasy and path-dependent ruin risk. Strong as the person who validates a strategy before capital touches it; less obviously the person who generates the strategy.
c09.interview_probe: Your submission says the most likely verdict is DEAD before you have measured anything. Suppose I re-measure and the ATR comes back at 250 points, not 450, and the trail turns out to be end-of-day on closed balance — so the arithmetic is uncomfortable but not fatal. Walk me through the next four weeks: what hypothesis do you actually test, what would make you say TRADE SMALL rather than NOT PROVEN, and what is the smallest out-of-sample evidence you would accept given that a daily NQ strategy will not generate 100 out-of-sample trades quickly?

c10.one_line: Leads with the risk-geometry arithmetic that kills the mandate ($2,000 = 100 NQ points vs ~400-point ATR) and backs it with a genuinely rigorous, pre-registered, power-first method — the strongest 'tell me honestly when it doesn't work' profile you will see, with an open question about whether it can ever find an edge rather than only disprove one.
strengths: Opens with the decisive number rather than a process description: $20/point × 100 points = the entire $2,000 budget, roughly a quarter of one NQ daily range, and explicitly notes the conclusion is insensitive to which ATR figure is right — a CEO can verify this without trusting the candidate.

Correctly identifies that the mandate's biggest unknown is the drawdown *type* (static / EOD trailing / intraday trailing on peak unrealized equity) and explains the ratchet mechanic: a trade that goes +80 and returns to flat can kill the account. Most candidates will treat '$2,000 max drawdown' as a single number.

Power analysis done with real numbers before any result: SE(SR) ≈ 0.32 on ten years of daily bars, 0.58 on three, and best-of-20 noise variants landing near Sharpe 1.2 — arithmetic that is actually correct and that pre-commits the candidate to a threshold.

Specific, non-generic data hygiene: signals on the back-adjusted series but risk and P&L in points on the unadjusted per-contract price; volume-crossover roll rather than fixed days-to-expiry; forcing the Globex-session vs RTH daily-bar choice up front instead of picking whichever backtests better.

Names the exact overfitting trap this mandate creates — searching for a rule whose stop happens to fit inside 100 points selects on in-sample maximum adverse excursion, the least stable statistic available — and fixes it by pre-registering the stop as an ATR multiple.

Reframes the deliverable as a survival/first-passage problem simulated bar-by-bar on 1-minute data under both trail variants, with the observation that a 65% hit-rate positive-expectancy system can still breach on over half of paths. That is the right test and is not the test most people run.
Separates 'passing the evaluation' from 'running funded capital' as different objective functions, and flags optimising one while reporting the other as a route to being confidently wrong.

Trial count treated as durable state (append-only committed trials.log surviving across sessions), which addresses the real-world leak where twenty variants over three weeks feel like one honest attempt.
concerns: The 'costs are irrelevant here, full stop' claim is the one piece of confidently wrong arithmetic in the submission. Costs are small against a 400-point ATR but not against a 100-point lifetime budget: at ~$20 round turn (1 point), the 30+ trades an evaluation's minimum-trading-day rule requires burns roughly a third of the total drawdown room. The candidate compared costs to the wrong denominator after correctly insisting the budget is the binding constraint.

Much of the framing — the 100-points-vs-410-450-ATR example, the MNQ 2.4× comparison, the four escalation options — is reproduced closely from the candidate's own standing operating instructions, so part of what reads as insight is a pre-loaded template being pattern-matched onto the brief. The genuinely new work (roll/P&L separation, MAE selection, first-passage framing, power numbers) is real, but weight the submission for that layer rather than the headline.

Every demonstrated spec is immediately disclaimed as something it would read from a source rather than know. Defensible discipline, but the brief asked for someone who knows the complex cold, and the candidate's self-description explicitly buys two months of elementary questions. Expect real latency on anything requiring desk intuition rather than measurement.

No options content at all — no IV, skew, VXN/realised spread, or how NQ options would inform the futures view. The task did not ask, so this is not a fault, but it leaves the second half of your brief entirely unevidenced.

The stated 'most likely productive result' is a documented no plus a pipeline. Nothing in the submission demonstrates hypothesis generation — where a candidate edge would come from, what market structure would motivate it. This profile is superbly equipped to falsify and unproven at proposing.

Process weight is high: specs.yaml, pre-registration, CSCV, purged walk-forward, block bootstrap and MC survival on every question. Excellent for a strategy that will be risked; potentially slow for the cheap screening pass that decides whether a hypothesis is worth that machinery. The submission mentions vectorbt pre-screening but does not budget for it.

Assumes a $3,000 profit target and 30-day/90-day evaluation horizon without flagging that the target-to-drawdown ratio is itself the feasibility question; it is listed as an open question but not carried into the arithmetic that leads the memo.
c10.distinctive: It computes the minimum detectable effect before looking at the result and states the threshold in writing, then treats the trailing-drawdown breach probability — not the Sharpe or the equity curve — as the deliverable. Almost every other candidate will describe a backtesting workflow; this one describes a measurement with a stated noise floor and a pre-committed way to be proven wrong, and it puts the number that kills the mandate in the first paragraph rather than the conclusion.
c10.best_used_for: Adjudicating strategies and mandates that someone else has proposed: feasibility and risk-geometry arithmetic before any research spend, path-dependent survival simulation under prop-firm drawdown rules, and forensic audit of a backtest that looks good — deflated Sharpe, trial accounting, roll and lookahead contamination, cost and fill sensitivity. It is the right agent to hand a promising result to before you risk money on it.
c10.interview_probe: Two parts. First: you said costs are irrelevant here — recompute that against the $2,000 budget rather than against ATR, given the evaluation's minimum-trading-days requirement, and tell me whether the answer changes. Second: assume I accept your feasibility verdict and move the mandate to MNQ at 1–10 lots, where the geometry closes. Give me the first three hypotheses you would test, in order, with the specific reason each one might exist in NQ — I want to see where an edge comes from, not only how you would kill it.
